name: Mendeleev leaves holes in the table
scope: The table whose power was PREDICTION. T1: in 1869 Mendeleev laid out the 63 known elements by increasing atomic weight — and did the thing no rival table did: he left EMPTY SQUARES, insisting undiscovered elements would arrive to fill them (Newlands' 1865 'law of octaves' and Lothar Meyer's 1870 curve sorted the same elements but staked nothing on blanks). T2: he did not just leave a hole, he described its tenant — 'eka-aluminium' would have atomic weight near 68, density near 5.9 g/cm3, and a chloride of formula ECl3. T3 (payoff): in 1875 Paul-Emile Lecoq de Boisbaudran, hunting with a spectroscope, saw two violet lines in zinc ore from the Pyrenees and named the new metal gallium — but measured its density as 4.7. Mendeleev, who had never held the sample, wrote to tell him the measurement was wrong; Boisbaudran repurified his gallium and got 5.904. T4: 1886, Clemens Winkler in Freiberg analysed a new silver mineral, argyrodite, and his totals only reached 93-94% — the missing 6% was an element. He first guessed it sat between antimony and bismuth; Mendeleev suggested eka-cadmium; Lothar Meyer said eka-silicon, and eka-silicon won. Predicted 72 / 5.5 / a chloride boiling under 100C; germanium delivered 72.6 / 5.47 / GeCl4 boiling at 86C. T4b: scandium, 1879 — Lars Fredrik Nilson isolated it without realising what it was; Per Teodor Cleve, working in the same institution, recognised it as eka-boron. T5: the honest caveat — Mendeleev also predicted elements that do not exist. In his 1904 'An Attempt Towards a Chemical Conception of the Ether' he proposed two elements LIGHTER than hydrogen, 'newtonium' (~0.17) and 'coronium' (~0.4), to carry the luminiferous ether. T5b: he got the argon news wrong too — his first response to Ramsay's inert gas in 1894 was to deny it was an element and propose it was triatomic nitrogen, N3, mass 42, rather than admit a whole new column; he accepted Group 0 by 1902. T5c: the crack in the foundation — tellurium (127.6) is heavier than iodine (126.9), yet Mendeleev put iodine second because their chemistry demanded it, and assumed the atomic weights had been mismeasured. They hadn't. The table's real ordering rule was not weight at all.
source: Grokipedia 'Dmitri Mendeleev' (1869 table of 63 elements, 6 March 1869 presentation via Menshutkin, the 1871 eka- predictions with numeric values, gallium/scandium/germanium matches, Te-I inversion, 1902 Group 0 revision, Davy Medal 1882, Nobel misses); Wikipedia 'Gallium' (Boisbaudran's two violet lines in Pyrenean sphalerite 1875, density 4.7 corrected to 5.904 after Mendeleev's letter, the Gallia/le-coq naming dispute); Wikipedia 'Clemens Winkler' and ChemTeam 'Discovery of Germanium' (argyrodite from the Himmelsfuerst mine, 93-94% mass shortfall, 6 Feb 1886, eka-antimony/eka-cadmium/eka-silicon dispute); Wikipedia + Grokipedia 'Mendeleev's predicted elements' (newtonium ~0.17 and coronium ~0.4 in the 1904 ether book; the N3 hypothesis for argon).
framing_note: The flagship PREDICTION ladder for the whole sub-strand and the spine every other chemistry topic hangs off. Voice: DISCOVERY mode at T1-T4, then a deliberate REVERSAL turn at T5 — the same man, the same method, wrong. T1 must key the ACT (he left blanks on purpose), never the date or the phrase 'periodic table'. Accuracy rail: state the predicted-vs-actual numbers exactly as sourced (eka-aluminium 68 / 5.9 vs gallium 69.72 / 5.91; eka-silicon 72 / 5.5 / bp<100C vs germanium 72.6 / 5.47 / 86C) and do NOT claim Mendeleev predicted the noble gases — he actively resisted them. Dinner-test payoff: T3, the letter that corrected a measurement from 2,000 miles away. Distractor mine: the real rival systems and their authors (Newlands' octaves, Lothar Meyer's atomic-volume curve, Doebereiner's triads, Chancourtois' telluric screw) plus the real wrong guesses about germanium's slot. Anti-restatement: never let a stem say 'the table predicts missing elements' before asking what Mendeleev did — describe the blank squares and the letter, and let the knowledge be recalled. Teach 'atomic weight' before testing it; do NOT introduce atomic number here — that is the Moseley ladder's payoff.
history_overlap: PHILOSOPHY bank: risky-prediction-vs-accommodation is a Popper/falsifiability seminar move that bank may own. Guard: every rung here must be anchored to a NAMED element and a MEASURED number (5.904, 86C, 93-94%), never to the abstract virtue of prediction. Internal SCIENCE overlap: the Te-I ordering anomaly and the N3-argon resistance are also live in the Moseley and Ramsay ladders — assign Te-I's RESOLUTION to Moseley and the argon resistance to Ramsay's reception rung; keep only the unresolved puzzle here.

name: Hennig Brand boils urine and finds cold fire
scope: The first element with a discoverer's name attached — found by a man hunting something else entirely. T1: in 1669 in Hamburg, Hennig Brand was not looking for a new element; he was looking for GOLD. He believed urine's golden colour meant it held the philosopher's stone, and he collected roughly fifty buckets of it from local beer-drinkers. T2: he let it putrefy for weeks, boiled it down over about a fortnight to a tar-like paste, mixed the residue with sand and charcoal and roasted it in a glass retort — and what condensed was a white waxy solid that glowed pale green in the dark WITHOUT heat. He called it 'cold fire' and named it phosphorus mirabilis, Greek for light-bearer. T3 (mechanism): the glow is not a flame. White phosphorus reacts slowly with oxygen in damp air and the reaction releases its energy as light rather than heat — chemiluminescence. Warm the same lump past about 30C and it stops glowing and simply bursts into flame, with a garlic smell and dense white smoke. T4: Brand treated the recipe as a trade secret, sold it to the merchant Johann Daniel Kraft for 200 thalers, and Johann Kunckel — who had only ever seen samples — reproduced it and sometimes claimed the discovery for himself. Robert Boyle worked out his own version and lodged a recipe with the Royal Society in 1680. Publication, not secrecy, is what turned a marvel into science. T5: why Brand counts at all — copper, gold, iron, sulfur, lead and carbon have no discoverer; they were simply always known. Brand is the first person in recorded history whose NAME attaches to the finding of an element. T5b: the coda — he died in obscurity around 1710, having sold his secret and never learned that the substance he pulled out of a bucket is the backbone of DNA, the P in ATP, and a third of the mineral in your bones.
source: Grokipedia 'Hennig Brand' (1669 Hamburg, ~50 buckets of beer-drinkers' urine, fermentation then ~2 weeks of boiling to a paste, sand/charcoal reduction in a retort, phosphorus mirabilis, ignition near 30C, garlic odour, secret sold to Daniel Kraft for 200 thalers, Kunckel's 1677 replication and priority claim, Boyle's 1680 recipe deposited with the Royal Society, death c.1710, Lavoisier's later classification as an element); Science History Institute, 'Hennig Brandt and the Discovery of Phosphorus'.
framing_note: Voice: DISCOVERY mode with the accidental-result twist — the wonder is that a wrong theory (the doctrine of signatures: yellow liquid must hide yellow metal) run with real patience produced a real element. T1 keys the GOAL and the buckets, never a date. Accuracy rail: do NOT say Brand 'discovered the element phosphorus' as though he understood what an element was — nobody did in 1669; Lavoisier classified phosphorus as an element more than a century later. Do not inflate the yield: an enormous volume of urine gave a small waxy lump. Do not say he let it rot 'for years'. Dinner-test payoff: T1/T2 (fifty buckets of urine, then a lump that glows in the dark without burning). Distractor mine: the real alchemical goals of the era (the philosopher's stone, the alkahest/universal solvent, the elixir of life) and the real rival claimants (Kunckel, Kraft, Boyle) — historically live answers a serious 17th-century reader would have picked. Anti-restatement: the stem may describe the urine, the retort and the green glow but must never name 'phosphorus' or 'light-bearer' before asking. Teach 'chemiluminescence' at T3 before any rung tests it.

name: Lavoisier weighs the world and phlogiston dies
scope: Careful WEIGHING beats a beloved theory. T1: for a century every chemist in Europe 'knew' that burning released a substance called phlogiston. Lavoisier's weapon was not a new idea — it was a balance fine enough to catch fractions of a grain and sealed glass vessels so that nothing could sneak in or out. T2 (payoff): the killer number. Seal a metal like tin in a glass vessel and heat it, and the ash — the 'calx' — comes out HEAVIER than the metal you started with, while the air in the vessel loses volume, and the two amounts match. If burning releases something, why does the burned thing gain weight? T3: the ad-hoc rescue that finished the theory off — defenders answered that phlogiston must have NEGATIVE weight. Lavoisier's 1783 memoir 'Reflexions sur le phlogistique' called it a 'veritable Proteus' that changed its properties whenever an experiment cornered it. A theory that can absorb any result explains nothing. T4: the mercury experiment — he heated mercury in a sealed apparatus for twelve days; a red calx crept over the surface and about one-fifth of the air disappeared; what was left smothered a candle and a mouse. Reheat the red calx and exactly that fifth came back out, and a candle blazed in it. T4b: the principle stated flat, in the Traite elementaire de chimie (1789): in every operation an equal quantity of matter exists before and after. T5: he got things badly wrong too. He named oxygen from the Greek for 'acid-former' because he was certain every acid must contain oxygen — Davy demolished that in 1810. And his own 1789 table of simple substances listed 'caloric' and 'light' as elements: the man who killed one weightless fluid kept two of his own. T5b: Marie-Anne Paulze Lavoisier learned English and Latin to translate the phlogistonists' own papers so he could answer them, engraved the plates of the apparatus for the Traite, and kept the laboratory's records. T5c: the dark coda — he was guillotined on 8 May 1794, not for his science but as a shareholder in the Ferme generale, the tax-farming company whose profits had paid for the laboratory. The line everyone quotes, 'the Republic has no need of savants', is apocryphal; what IS documented is Lagrange's remark the next day that it took only an instant to cut off that head, and a hundred years may not produce another like it.
source: Grokipedia 'Antoine Lavoisier' (sealed-vessel calcination of tin/lead from 1772, balances sensitive to fractions of a grain, mercury-calx work 1774-75, one-fifth of the air consumed, the 1783 'Reflexions sur le phlogistique' and the 'veritable Proteus' charge, the 1789 Traite statement of mass conservation, oxygene named for acid-formation in 1777, Ferme generale shareholding, guillotined 8 May 1794); Jean-Pierre Poirier via multiple secondary summaries establishing the 'the Republic has no need of scientists' line as APOCRYPHAL (Coffinhal refused Hallé's report to the tribunal; no record of the quote); ChemTeam 'Early acid-base theories' and Wikipedia 'Humphry Davy' for the 1810 refutation of the oxygen-acid rule.
framing_note: The sub-strand's flagship REVERSAL-BY-MEASUREMENT ladder, and the place the bank teaches what an ad-hoc rescue looks like. T1 keys the INSTRUMENT (a balance and a sealed jar), not a date or a definition of phlogiston. Accuracy rails, both load-bearing: (1) the 'Republic has no need of savants' line is APOCRYPHAL — build a rung that tells it AS a myth and gives the documented Lagrange remark instead; a rung whose answer is the fake quote is a bank bug. (2) Lavoisier did NOT discover oxygen — Scheele made it first, Priestley published first; Lavoisier named and explained it. Dinner-test payoff: T2, the ash that weighs more than the metal. Distractor mine: the richest in the sub-strand — phlogiston itself, caloric, the four classical elements, 'fixed air', 'dephlogisticated air', negative-weight phlogiston. Every distractor should be a position a serious 1780s chemist actually held. Anti-restatement: never let a stem say 'burning is combination with oxygen' before asking what the balance showed. Teach 'calx' and 'conservation of mass' in-rung before any later rung leans on them. The T5 caloric-and-light rung is the self-skepticism payoff — do not soften it.
history_overlap: PHILOSOPHY bank: the unfalsifiable-theory / ad-hoc-rescue move (negative-weight phlogiston, the 'Proteus' charge) is Popper territory that bank may own as a seminar concept. Guard: every rung here stays inside the laboratory — a specific substance, a specific weighing, a named memoir. HISTORY bank: the French Revolution and the Terror — cede the politics; the guillotine rung is one coda anchored on the Ferme generale and the apocryphal quote, not on revolutionary history.

name: Oxygen's three discoverers
scope: A messy priority fight where all three men have a real claim, and none of them is 'the discoverer'. T1: on 1 August 1774 Joseph Priestley focused sunlight through a burning lens onto a sample of red mercuric oxide and collected the gas that came off. A candle in it flared with startling brilliance — he wrote that he had found 'an air five or six times as good as common air'. T2 (payoff): he tested it the way you would. He put a mouse in a sealed jar of it, and the mouse lived far longer than it should have in that volume of ordinary air. Then he breathed it himself, and recorded that his chest felt 'peculiarly light and easy' for some time afterwards. T3: he had already glimpsed the other half of the story. In 1771-72 he showed that a candle burned out in a sealed jar, but a sprig of MINT left living in that jar for days restored the air so that a candle would burn in it again — photosynthesis, seen without the concept. The Royal Society gave him the Copley Medal for it in 1773. T4: the man who got there first got nothing. The Swedish apothecary Carl Wilhelm Scheele had made the same gas in 1771-72 and called it 'fire air'. His manuscript reached the printer in 1775, but 'Chemische Abhandlung von der Luft und dem Feuer' did not appear until 1777, by which time Priestley and Lavoisier had both published. Priority in science is not about who knew first; it is about who published first. T4b: in October 1774, in Paris, Priestley described his new air to Lavoisier over dinner and repeated the experiment for him. Lavoisier ran it with a balance and drew a conclusion Priestley never would. T5: Priestley never gave up phlogiston. He called his gas 'dephlogisticated air' to the end of his life in 1804 and argued against Lavoisier's whole system — the man who made the gas rejected what it meant. T5b: in July 1791 a Birmingham mob burned his house and laboratory over his politics and religion, and he emigrated to Pennsylvania in 1794.
source: Grokipedia 'Joseph Priestley' (isolation of dephlogisticated air, the mint/restored-air observation, lifelong adherence to phlogiston, the 1791 Priestley Riots, emigration 1794, the shared-credit framing with Scheele and Lavoisier); APS Physics History 'August 1774: Priestley isolates a new air' (1 August 1774, burning lens on mercuric oxide, candle and mouse, 'five or six times as good as common air'); Britannica 'Joseph Priestley' (Copley Medal 1773; the October 1774 Paris dinner with Lavoisier); Wikipedia 'Carl Wilhelm Scheele' and 'Fire air' (fire air prepared c.1771-72, manuscript to the printer Swederus 1775, published 1777, priority lost).
framing_note: Voice: DISCOVERY plus a genuine MYSTERY-of-credit rung — the bank refuses to crown a single discoverer. The honest statement, which should be a rung's answer and not a stem's giveaway: Scheele made it first, Priestley published first, Lavoisier understood it first. Accuracy rails: Priestley's own quoted words are documented ('five or six times as good as common air'; 'peculiarly light and easy') — quote them exactly or not at all; and do not have Priestley 'discover oxygen' as a named element, he made 'dephlogisticated air'. Dinner-test payoff: T2, the mouse and then his own lungs — the self-test that the sub-strand's soul rewards. Distractor mine: the real rival airs and their makers (fixed air/Black, inflammable air/Cavendish, phlogisticated air, fire air/Scheele) and the three real claimants themselves — a distractor of 'Lavoisier' on the T1 rung is exactly the productive kind of wrong. Anti-restatement: the stem describes the lens, the red powder, the flaring candle; it must never say 'oxygen'. LANE BORDER: the mint-jar rung is Priestley's air chemistry, not plant biology — keep it on the candle relighting, never on how a leaf works.
history_overlap: HISTORY bank: the 1791 Priestley Riots and Dissenter politics in Birmingham, and Priestley's support for the American and French Revolutions, belong to history — cap this ladder at ONE coda rung on the burned laboratory and keep it framed as what it cost a working chemist.

name: Davy's battery tears new metals out of rock
scope: A brand-new instrument opens a seam nobody could reach. T1: in October 1807 Humphry Davy ran the current from the Royal Institution's enormous voltaic battery through molten caustic potash. Tiny silvery globules burst up through the crust and caught fire the instant they touched the air. His cousin Edmund, who was assisting, wrote that Davy 'danced about the room in ecstatic delight' and had to be calmed before the experiment could go on. T2 (mechanism): why nobody had done it before. Potash and soda are the ASHES — the metal in them holds oxygen so tightly that no furnace, acid or reducing agent could pry it away. Electricity could, because it does the chemistry with raw electric force instead of a competing chemical. T3: he named them for their sources — potassium from potash, sodium from soda — and announced both in the Bakerian Lecture to the Royal Society on 19 November 1807. T4: he did it again the next year. Calcium, magnesium, strontium and barium came out of lime, magnesia, strontia and baryta, announced 30 June 1808. The 'earths' that every chemist had classed as elements turned out to be oxides of metals no one had ever seen. T4b: he had already made himself the instrument. At Beddoes's Pneumatic Institution in Bristol in 1799 he inhaled nitrous oxide in over 160 sessions, logged his pulse climbing from 66 to 104, gave the stuff the name 'laughing gas', noted that it killed the pain of an inflamed gum — and got Coleridge and Southey to try it. Surgery ignored the hint for more than forty years. T5: 1810 — Davy showed that 'oxymuriatic acid gas' was not the oxide of some unknown element but an element in its own right, and named it chlorine. Muriatic acid turned out to be hydrogen and chlorine with no oxygen at all, which destroyed Lavoisier's rule that oxygen is what makes an acid an acid. T5b: what self-experimenting cost him. In 1799 he inhaled 'water gas' — hydrogen and carbon monoxide — and nearly died. In November 1812 a nitrogen trichloride explosion, from a fragment he described as 'scarcely bigger than a pin's head', wounded his eyes. Needing someone to write for him, he took on a bookbinder's apprentice named Michael Faraday. T5c: the miners' lamp, 1815 — wire gauze around a flame carries heat away fast enough that the flame cannot pass through to the firedamp outside. Davy refused to patent it.
source: Grokipedia 'Humphry Davy' (Pneumatic Institution 1798-1801, 160+ nitrous oxide sessions April-June 1799, pulse 66->104, 'laughing gas', the 1800 'Researches' monograph, the near-fatal water-gas inhalation, electrolysis of molten KOH and NaOH with a large voltaic pile, Bakerian Lecture 19 Nov 1807, the alkaline earths announced 30 June 1808, the 1815 safety lamp); todayinsci 'Edmund Davy' and the Chemistry World potassium podcast (the 'minute globules... danced about the room in ecstatic delight' account, from Edmund Davy as assistant); Wikipedia 'Humphry Davy' + ChemTeam 'Early acid-base theories' (chlorine named an element 1810; muriatic acid shown oxygen-free; the 16 Nov 1812 NCl3 injury letter to John Children; Faraday hired 1813).
framing_note: Voice: DISCOVERY mode, and the sub-strand's clearest case of a NEW TOOL opening a locked door. T1 keys the visible moment (globules bursting through the crust and igniting) plus the reaction of the man watching — never a date, never 'who discovered potassium'. Accuracy rails: the 'danced about the room in ecstatic delight' account is Edmund Davy's, recorded second-hand — attribute it to his cousin's account rather than presenting it as Davy's own words; and Davy's own November 1812 letter says the fragment was 'scarcely bigger than a pin's head' and that he expected his sight to recover, so do NOT write that he was blinded. Dinner-test payoff: T1 (a man dancing round his own laboratory) and T4b (he tested laughing gas on himself 160 times). Distractor mine: real rival techniques of the day (furnace reduction with charcoal, reduction by potassium amalgam, acid dissolution) and real adjacent chemists (Berzelius, Gay-Lussac and Thenard, Oersted, Berthollet). Anti-restatement: never let a stem say 'electrolysis frees reactive metals' before asking what Davy did — describe the molten potash, the battery and the burning globules. Teach 'electrolysis' and 'voltaic pile' in-rung before testing them.
history_overlap: Internal SCIENCE overlap: an anaesthesia/medicine sub-strand may own Morton's 1846 ether demonstration — keep this ladder on Davy's own 1799 self-experiment and on the forty-year gap before anyone acted on it, and cede the operating-theatre story. The Faraday hiring is a coda here only; a Faraday/electromagnetism ladder owns Faraday himself. HISTORY bank: Victorian mine disasters and the Davy-vs-Stephenson lamp priority dispute — cede both; keep the lamp rung on the gauze mechanism.

name: Reading elements in a beam of light
scope: CONCEPT ladder: the spectroscope turns light into a name, and the discipline it took to trust it. T1: in 1860 in Heidelberg, Robert Bunsen and Gustav Kirchhoff dripped mineral water from the springs at Duerkheim into a flame and looked through a prism. Two brilliant sky-blue lines appeared that matched no known element. They named it caesium, from the Latin caesius, sky-blue — the first element in history found by its light rather than its substance. T2: what it cost to prove. To get a weighable sample they evaporated 44,000 litres of that spring water down to 240 kilograms of concentrated salts — and out of all of it came about 7.3 grams of caesium chloride. T2b: they did it again the next year — two deep red lines in a lithium mineral gave rubidium, from rubidus, deep red. Elements had begun announcing themselves by colour. T3 (mechanism): a hot thin gas emits light only at the wavelengths its own atoms can emit, so every element has a fixed pattern of lines — a barcode that does not change with distance or quantity. That is why a prism can identify a substance nobody will ever touch. T4 (payoff): on 18 August 1868, during a total solar eclipse observed from Guntur in India, Pierre Janssen found a bright yellow line in the Sun's chromosphere lying near, but not on, sodium's. Norman Lockyer saw it from London that October and with Edward Frankland argued it belonged to an element unknown on Earth. They named it helium, after helios, the Sun. T4b: for 27 years helium was an element with no earthly sample. In 1895 William Ramsay treated the uranium mineral cleveite with acid, collected the gas that came off, and there was the 587.49 nm yellow line — the Sun's element in a London flask (Cleve and Langlet in Uppsala found it almost simultaneously). T5: the method's dark twin. A strange green line in nebulae, first seen by William Huggins in 1864, was pinned on an element called 'nebulium'; odd lines in the Sun's corona were pinned on 'coronium'. Neither element exists. In 1927 Ira Bowen showed the nebular lines are FORBIDDEN transitions of doubly ionised oxygen, possible only at densities no laboratory on Earth can reach. T5b: in 1941 Bengt Edlen identified the coronal green line at 5303 angstroms as iron stripped of thirteen electrons — which meant the Sun's corona is at more than a million degrees. A false element had been hiding a real and shocking measurement. T5c: the rule spectroscopists paid for — an unfamiliar line is evidence of an unfamiliar STATE at least as often as an unfamiliar element.
source: Wikipedia 'Caesium' (1860 Duerkheim mineral water, 44,000 litres -> 240 kg of salts -> 7.3 g caesium chloride; caesius = bluish-grey/sky-blue; first element discovered with a spectroscope); Science History Institute 'Robert Bunsen and Gustav Kirchhoff'; University of Waterloo 'Spectroscopy 1855-1864' (rubidium 1861, thallium, indium); Grokipedia 'Helium' (587.49 nm yellow line seen 1868 by Janssen and Lockyer during the eclipse, named from helios, first element identified extraterrestrially; Ramsay and Travers isolating it from cleveite in 1895); Wikipedia 'Nebulium' and 'Ira Sprague Bowen' (Huggins 1864 green line; Bowen 1927 forbidden [O III]; Russell's 'nebulium has vanished into thin air'); Nature 150, 756 'Origin of the Coronium Lines' and Encyclopedia.com 'Edlen, Bengt' (1941 identification of 5303 A as Fe XIV, red 6374 A as Fe X).
framing_note: The sub-strand's analytic backbone and its best MYSTERY-then-resolution arc. Shape B: one method deepened across the named cases that display it. T1 keys the ACT and the colour (sky-blue lines in spring water), not the word 'spectroscopy'. Teach 'spectral line' and 'emission spectrum' explicitly at T3 before any rung leans on them. Accuracy rails: Janssen and Lockyer worked INDEPENDENTLY and both have a real claim — never write 'Lockyer discovered helium' unqualified; and the 1868 line was seen in the Sun's chromosphere during an eclipse, not 'in sunlight generally'. On the nebulium/coronium rungs, follow the MYSTERY rule strictly: state plainly that the lines were real and the elements were not, and never let a distractor secretly be the truth. Dinner-test payoff: T4 — an element found on the Sun 27 years before anyone had a sample on Earth. Distractor mine: the real ghost elements (nebulium, coronium, and Mendeleev's newtonium) alongside real elements found by spectroscope (thallium, indium, rubidium) — every wrong option is something a competent 19th-century observer proposed.
history_overlap: Internal SCIENCE overlap: an astronomy sub-strand very likely owns Fraunhofer's dark absorption lines, stellar composition, and the million-degree corona as a solar-physics puzzle. Guard: this ladder is ELEMENT-HUNTING only — caesium, rubidium, helium, and the two ghost elements. State the corona temperature only as the payoff of Edlen's identification, one rung, and do not tour the Sun. The 1895 cleveite isolation is shared with the Ramsay noble-gas ladder — put the SOLAR-line-matched-on-Earth framing here and the missing-column framing there so the two rungs test different facts.

name: Ramsay finds a whole column nobody suspected
scope: A discrepancy of half a percent that a lazier chemist would have called measurement error. T1 (payoff): Lord Rayleigh weighed a litre of nitrogen made by chemical reaction: 1.2505 grams. Then a litre of nitrogen taken from ordinary AIR by stripping out the oxygen, water and carbon dioxide: 1.2572 grams. Same gas, two different weights. One of them was not pure nitrogen. T2: Rayleigh could not account for it, and in 1892 he published a letter in Nature asking anyone at all for an explanation. William Ramsay heard him lecture on 19 April 1894 and asked leave to hunt the difference down. T3 (method): Ramsay passed air-nitrogen over red-hot magnesium again and again. The magnesium ate the nitrogen as magnesium nitride, the volume kept shrinking, and the density of what was left kept RISING — 22 litres at density 14, then 1.5 litres at 16.1, then a stubborn final 290 cubic centimetres at density 19.95 that would react with nothing at all. They announced it in August 1894 and named it argon, Greek for 'lazy'. T3b: Henry Cavendish had seen it in 1785. Sparking air with excess oxygen, he was left with a small residue, no more than about a hundred-and-twentieth of the original, that refused to combine with anything. He wrote it down honestly and it sat unexplained for 109 years. T4: in 1895 Ramsay pulled helium out of the mineral cleveite — and now he had TWO gases that reacted with nothing and had no home in the periodic table. Two orphans is not an anomaly; it is a missing COLUMN. T4b: in the summer of 1898, with Morris Travers, he liquefied argon and boiled it off in stages — krypton ('hidden') in May, neon ('new') in June, xenon ('stranger') in July. Travers on the moment neon's discharge tube lit: 'The blaze of crimson light from the tube told its own story, and it was a sight to dwell upon and never to forget.' T5 (mechanism): why they react with nothing — a full outer shell of electrons leaves them nothing to gain or share. The table's most consequential column is the one you cannot see, smell or taste, and argon is about 1% of the air in the room. T5b: the establishment's answer to the news — Mendeleev's first response was to deny argon was an element at all, proposing that it was triatomic nitrogen, N3, mass 42, rather than accept a whole new group. He came round and added Group 0 in 1902. T5c: in 1904 both men took Nobel Prizes in the same year for the same discovery — Rayleigh in Physics, Ramsay in Chemistry; Ramsay went on to isolate radon in 1910.
source: Wikipedia 'William Ramsay' (Rayleigh's 19 April 1894 lecture, the density discrepancy, argon announced August 1894, cleveite helium 1895, neon/krypton/xenon 1898 with Travers, radon 1910, the paired 1904 Nobels); Le Moyne (Giunta), 'The Discovery of Argon: a Case Study in Scientific Method' (1.2505 vs 1.2572 g per litre; the magnesium-nitride method with the 22 L / 1.5 L / 290 cm3 density series ending at 19.95; Cavendish's 1785 residue of about 1/120-1/125); APS Physics History 'Lord Rayleigh and the Discovery of Argon'; Science History Institute 'A Blaze of Crimson Light: The Story of Neon' (Travers' quotation; krypton May, neon June, xenon July 1898); Grokipedia 'Mendeleev's predicted elements' (his N3 hypothesis for argon).
framing_note: Voice: DISCOVERY mode built on a MEASUREMENT anomaly — the purest 'take your own error bars seriously' story in the sub-strand. T1 must invert the wonder: put the two weights in the stem as the hook and make the consequence the answer. Accuracy rails: Rayleigh and Ramsay SHARE the credit (the paired 1904 Nobels are the proof) — no rung may imply Ramsay found argon alone; and Cavendish did NOT discover argon — he recorded an unexplained residue and claimed no element, which is precisely why the rung is worth having. The Travers quotation is documented; reproduce it exactly or paraphrase, never invent around it. Dinner-test payoff: T1 (half a percent) and T4b (the crimson tube). Distractor mine: the real explanations floated at the time for the density gap — a heavier allotrope of nitrogen, contamination of the sample, an undetected nitrogen-hydrogen compound, an error in Rayleigh's apparatus — every one of them a respectable 1894 guess. Teach 'inert' / 'full outer shell' at T5 before testing it; do not introduce electron shells earlier.
history_overlap: Internal SCIENCE overlap: the 1895 cleveite helium isolation is also a rung in the spectroscope ladder — keep the framing distinct (there: the Sun's line matched on Earth; here: a second orphan proving a whole column is missing). The Mendeleev-resists-argon fact is also live in the Mendeleev's-gaps ladder — assign it HERE as the discovery's reception and drop it there.

name: Moseley counts the charges and re-orders the table
scope: The number the table was really sorted by, found by firing electrons at metal. T1: in 1913-14 Henry Moseley fired electrons at one pure element after another and photographed the X-rays each one threw back. Laid side by side, the lines climbed in a perfectly regular staircase — one step per element, no half-steps and no missing steps allowed. T2: the quantity that made the staircase regular was NOT atomic weight. The square root of the X-ray frequency rose in equal steps with a whole number, and that whole number was the count of positive charges in the nucleus. Atomic NUMBER, not atomic mass, is what the periodic table is ordered by. T3 (payoff): that resolved the anomalies Mendeleev had papered over and apologised for. Tellurium is heavier than iodine; cobalt is heavier than nickel — and in each pair the heavier element still comes FIRST, because it has fewer protons. Mendeleev had put them in the right order for the right chemical reason and the wrong stated reason, and had wrongly blamed the atomic weights on bad measurement. T4: because the staircase allowed no gaps, Moseley could point straight at the holes: elements 43, 61, 72 and 75 had to exist, and nothing else could be squeezed in between the steps. He also settled a live argument by showing there was room for exactly fourteen rare earths and no more — the table stopped being a matter of judgement and became a matter of counting. T5: Moseley volunteered for the British Army and was shot dead by a sniper at Gallipoli on 10 August 1915, aged 27. He had done the work in about two years, and the Nobel Prize is not awarded posthumously.
source: Wikipedia "Moseley's law" and Grokipedia "Moseley's law" (the 1913-14 X-ray experiments, sqrt(frequency) linear in Z, atomic number rather than atomic mass as the ordering principle, the Fe-Co-Ni correction, the vacant slot at 43); NIST, 'Henry Moseley and the Periodic Table of the Elements'; Royal Society, Phil. Trans. A 378 (2020) 20190302, 'Henry Moseley, X-ray spectroscopy and the periodic table'; Grokipedia 'Dmitri Mendeleev' (Moseley 1913 resolving the atomic-weight inconsistencies).
framing_note: Voice: DISCOVERY plus a clean REVERSAL of what everyone thought the table's ordering rule was. T1 keys the METHOD picture (fire electrons at a metal, photograph the X-rays, watch a staircase appear), never a date or 'who discovered atomic number'. Accuracy rails: do not write Moseley's law as a formula to be memorised — the bank bans rote; state it as 'equal steps in the square root of the frequency, one step per element'. Do not say he 'discovered the proton' — he measured nuclear charge; Rutherford's group named the proton later. Teach 'nucleus' and 'nuclear charge' in-rung before testing 'atomic number'. Dinner-test payoff: T3 — cobalt outweighs nickel and still comes first, and now there is a reason. Distractor mine: the real competing ordering principles chemists had defended (atomic weight, valence, specific heat, position by chemical family) and real adjacent physicists (Rutherford, Barkla, Bohr, the Braggs). Anti-restatement: never let a stem contain the phrase 'number of protons' before asking what the staircase counted.
history_overlap: HISTORY bank: the Gallipoli campaign and Britain's use of scientists as infantry in WWI. Guard: exactly ONE coda rung on Moseley's death, anchored to his age and the two-year working life, never to the campaign; cede the war to history. Internal SCIENCE overlap: the Mendeleev's-gaps ladder raises the tellurium-iodine anomaly as an unsolved crack — its RESOLUTION belongs here and must not be duplicated there.

name: Aluminium: from an emperor's cutlery to a throwaway can
scope: The metal whose price fell by a factor of a thousand because someone found a new way to melt a rock. T1: the metal Napoleon III reserved for his most honoured guests was not gold. The story told is that his best guests ate with ALUMINIUM while the rest of the table made do with gold and silver — in the 1850s aluminium was the most expensive metal on Earth. T2 (mechanism): the paradox. Aluminium is the third most abundant element in the Earth's crust, about 8% by mass, and the commonest metal in it — but it never occurs as metal. Its grip on oxygen is so strong that ordinary smelting cannot break it. Abundance and availability are completely different things. T3: Friedrich Woehler got a grey powder in 1827. Henri Sainte-Claire Deville managed real ingots by 1854-55 using sodium, itself fabulously expensive, and showed twelve small bars at the 1855 Paris Exposition Universelle billed as silver made from clay. T4: in 1884 the very tip of the Washington Monument was capped with a 100-ounce cast aluminium pyramid, eight inches tall, the largest single piece of aluminium yet made. Aluminium ran about $1.10 an ounce when a manufacturing worker earned roughly $1.34 a DAY, and Tiffany's put the pyramid in its New York window first so people could say afterwards that they had stepped over the top of the Washington Monument. T5 (payoff): in 1886 Charles Martin Hall in Ohio and Paul Heroult in France, both twenty-two, independently hit the same trick within months of each other — dissolve alumina in molten cryolite, which lets it melt far below its own melting point, then run current through it. Add Karl Bayer's 1889 process for getting pure alumina out of bauxite and the price collapsed. Within a generation the emperor's metal was a disposable wrapper. T5b: the modern echo — pulling aluminium out of ore is so electricity-hungry that recycling it takes roughly 5% of the energy, which is why over three-quarters of all the aluminium ever produced is still in use.
source: Grokipedia 'Aluminium' (8.1% of the crust and the most abundant metallic element; Oersted 1825 and Woehler's early work; the Hall-Heroult process independently in 1886 by Hall and Heroult transforming aluminium from a metal once more valuable than gold into an industrial staple; over 75% of all aluminium ever produced still in use; recycling at ~5% of primary energy); Wikipedia 'History of aluminium' and 'Aluminium' (Deville's first industrial production; the twelve ingots at the 1855 Exposition Universelle; the reputed Napoleon III banquet); G. Binczewski, 'A History of the Aluminum Cap of the Washington Monument', JOM 47:11 (1995) and NPS 'The Point of the Matter' (100 oz cast pyramid, 1884, aluminium at $1.10/oz, Frishmuth billed $225, Tiffany's display).
framing_note: Voice: a REVERSAL of value rather than of theory — the wonder is that a metal's worth is set by the DIFFICULTY of freeing it, not by how rare its atoms are. T1 inverts the wonder: the astonishing fact (guests eating off aluminium while everyone else got gold) sits in the stem. Accuracy rails, both required: (1) the Napoleon III banquet is a widely repeated but REPUTED anecdote — write it as 'the story told is' / 'reputedly', never as documented fact; (2) keep the Washington Monument numbers honest — 100 ounces, about $1.10 an ounce for the metal, $225 for the whole commission — do not inflate the cap into a fortune. Dinner-test payoff: T4 (the cap cost about what a labourer earned in three months, and it sat in a jeweller's window) and T5 (two 22-year-olds on two continents, the same year). Distractor mine: real adjacent chemists and processes (Woehler, Oersted, Deville, sodium reduction, the Bayer process, Davy who named the element) and real rival 'precious' metals of the 1850s. Teach 'electrolysis' by reference to the Davy ladder rather than re-teaching it.
history_overlap: GEOGRAPHY bank: bauxite-producing regions and the places aluminium smelters cluster (cheap hydroelectric power) are place-anchored resource geography that bank may own — keep every rung here on the metallurgy, the price and the two 1886 inventors, and do not tour mining countries. Internal SCIENCE overlap: Davy named the element and coined 'alumium' — that fact belongs to the Davy ladder only as a passing name, not a rung in either place.

name: The Radium Craze
scope: Wonder without skepticism, and what it cost. T1: for roughly thirty years after 1898, radium was sold as a health product — glowing wristwatch dials, 'Revigator' crocks that made your drinking water radioactive overnight, Doramad radioactive toothpaste, Tho-Radia face cream. Glowing was advertised as vitality. T2: the flagship product was Radithor, radium dissolved in water, made by William J. A. Bailey, a Harvard dropout who styled himself a doctor. The Pittsburgh industrialist and amateur golf champion Eben Byers drank nearly 1,400 bottles between 1927 and 1930 because he was convinced it made him feel wonderful. T3 (mechanism, the heart of the ladder): radium sits directly below calcium in Group 2 of the periodic table, so the body handles it like calcium and files it in BONE — where it keeps emitting alpha particles for the rest of your life, radium-226's half-life being about 1,600 years. Byers lost most of his jaw and died in 1932. T4: from 1917 hundreds of young women at the US Radium Corporation and its competitors painted luminous 'Undark' numbers on watch and instrument dials, and were TAUGHT to point the brush with their lips between strokes — lip, dip, paint. Their jaws crumbled. T4b: why it took a decade to stop. Company-retained experts produced reassuring findings, and the women's illnesses were at first attributed to syphilis. Grace Fryer and four co-workers sued anyway; the newspapers called it the case of the five women doomed to die and it settled in 1928. Sabin von Sochocky, who invented the paint, died of it too. T5: the honest complication the bank must not skip — radium really does kill cells, which is why it was genuinely used in early cancer therapy and why radium-223 dichloride is an approved treatment TODAY for prostate cancer that has spread to bone. The same property that made it lethal in a tonic makes it a targeted drug. T5b: what was actually missing was not a law but a TEST. The products were legal, advertised, endorsed and popular; nobody had asked the one question — what happens to an alpha emitter once it is inside your skeleton, permanently? T5c: Marie Curie's laboratory notebooks are still so contaminated that they are kept in lead-lined boxes and readers sign a waiver before opening them.
source: Grokipedia 'Radium' (Ra-226 half-life ~1,600 years, alkaline-earth chemistry and calcium mimicry, ~1 g per 7 tons of ore, luminous paints and tonics leading to anaemia, bone necrosis and osteosarcoma, radium-223 dichloride approved for bone metastases in castration-resistant prostate cancer); Wikipedia 'Eben Byers' (nearly 1,400 bottles of Radithor, Bailey as a Harvard dropout falsely claiming an MD, loss of most of the jaw, death 31 March 1932, the FTC cease-and-desist of 19 December 1931); Wikipedia 'Grace Fryer' and HistoryNet 'The Radium Girls vs US Radium' (USRC Orange NJ from April 1917, the 'lip, dip, paint' instruction, 'Undark', the five plaintiffs, the 1928 settlement, Sabin von Sochocky's own death in 1928); ORAU Museum of Radiation and Radioactivity, 'Radithor'.
framing_note: This is the sub-strand's ONE stance ladder and the reason vision_mandated is true: the bank's claim that expert endorsement, legality and popularity are not evidence — only a test is. PRESENT, never preach. No rung may generalise about corporations, regulators or capitalism; every rung names a SPECIFIC act (Bailey's fake doctorate, the company-retained experts' reassuring reports, the supervisor's lip-pointing instruction, Fryer's decision to sue anyway). Accuracy rails: (1) Byers drank ~1,400 bottles over about three years and died in 1932 — do not conflate him with the dial painters, and do not imply a single dose killed him; (2) the T5 rung stating radium's real, current medical use is MANDATORY — the ladder must not leave a kid thinking radiation medicine is quackery. The bank's own skepticism rule applies to the bank: the corrective is 'they never ran the test', not 'science was wrong'. Dinner-test payoff: T3 — your body cannot tell radium from calcium and stores it in your bones for good. Distractor mine: the real contemporary explanations offered for the dial painters' illness (syphilis, phossy jaw from phosphorus matches, 'neurasthenia', poor dentistry) and the real rival radium products. Do not use images or scenarios that dwell on the women's suffering; keep it clinical and specific, grade-appropriate.
history_overlap: HISTORY bank (dark chapters): the Radium Girls litigation, US Radium Corporation's conduct and the resulting labour and workers'-compensation law is history's episode — if history owns the courtroom, cede the 1928 settlement rung and keep this ladder on the calcium-mimicry mechanism, the consumer craze and the missing test. Internal SCIENCE overlap: a Curie ladder elsewhere in the bank owns the 1898 discovery and the pitchblende labour — this ladder must NOT re-tell the discovery; it starts after it, which is why tier_span begins at T2.

name: The periodic table in your pocket
scope: CONCEPT ladder: a phone is a pocket periodic table, and each element is in there for one specific physical reason. T1: a modern smartphone contains something like two-thirds of the stable elements on the periodic table — around sixty of them — in a slab you can hold in one hand. T2 (payoff): the touchscreen works because of indium. Indium tin oxide is one of the very few materials that is BOTH electrically conductive and transparent, so it can carry the signal of your finger across the glass without you ever seeing the wiring. T3: the speaker and the vibration motor run on neodymium-iron-boron magnets, the strongest permanent magnets known, with dysprosium and praseodymium added so they do not lose their strength when the phone gets hot. That combination is why a phone can be a few millimetres thick and still move air loudly enough to hear. T3b: the colours come from rare-earth phosphors — europium and terbium among them — sitting in front of a white backlight, because a screen needs pure reds and greens that ordinary materials will not give. T4: tantalum. Its oxide layer is such a good insulator that a tantalum capacitor stores far more charge per unit of volume than the alternatives, which is the reason the electronics fit inside the case at all. T4b: the glass is aluminosilicate soaked in molten potassium salt, so that large potassium ions swap into sites left by smaller sodium ions and jam the surface into permanent compression — a crack has to fight that compression before it can spread. T5: gallium closes the loop. Silicon can compute but is very poor at emitting light and at handling very high radio frequencies, so gallium arsenide and gallium nitride do the antenna and the LEDs. Gallium is Mendeleev's eka-aluminium — the element he described before anyone had seen it is the reason your phone can talk to a tower. T5b: none of these is mined as itself. Gallium, indium and germanium are all BY-PRODUCTS of refining zinc, aluminium and copper, so their supply is set by the markets for entirely different metals.
source: Compound Interest, 'The Chemical Elements of a Smartphone' (aluminosilicate glass with molten-salt potassium ion exchange; indium tin oxide as the transparent conductive touch layer; rare-earth screen phosphors; silicon chip with phosphorus/arsenic/boron/gallium dopants; tantalum as the main component of micro-capacitors; tungsten contacts; neodymium-iron-boron magnets with dysprosium and praseodymium for speakers, microphones and vibration motors; lithium/cobalt/graphite battery); Visual Capitalist 'Critical Metals in a Smartphone' and World Economic Forum coverage of the University of Birmingham breakdown (~60+ elements, roughly two-thirds of the stable elements); Wikipedia 'Gallium' (gallium as a by-product of zinc and aluminium processing; GaAs and GaN in RF and optoelectronics).
framing_note: Shape B theme ladder and the sub-strand's 'go look at the thing in your hand' invitation. Every rung must be ELEMENT -> PROPERTY -> JOB, in that order, with the job as the answer's anchor: no rung may answer 'a rare metal' or 'a semiconductor'. T1 inverts the wonder with the count (two-thirds of the stable elements) and makes the object the answer. Accuracy rails: give the element counts as approximate and sourced ('around sixty', 'roughly two-thirds of the stable elements') — exact totals vary by model and by who is counting; and do not claim any single element is irreplaceable, since substitutes exist for several. Dinner-test payoff: T2 — a transparent conductor is why glass can be a button. Distractor mine: real adjacent materials that ALMOST do the job (copper and silver, which conduct but are opaque; iron and ferrite magnets, which are weaker; aluminium electrolytic capacitors; silicon for RF) — every wrong answer is a real engineering option that loses for a stateable reason. Ties back to the Mendeleev ladder at T5; state gallium's eka-aluminium identity only there.
history_overlap: GEOGRAPHY bank: place-anchored resource geography — DRC coltan and the conflict-minerals story, Chinese dominance of rare-earth refining, lithium in the Atacama — is geography's lane. Guard: at most ONE mention of coltan/DRC, framed as where tantalum's ore comes from, and never as a politics rung; cede the whole where-it-comes-from tour. Internal SCIENCE overlap: the tungsten-contacts detail is also live in the tungsten filament ladder — keep tungsten out of this ladder's rung set to avoid a duplicate fact.

name: Tungsten, the filament that would not melt
scope: The element chosen for one number, and the two problems that were not that number. T1: Edison's carbon filaments burned dim and died fast because carbon evaporates away at the temperature that makes useful light. The answer was the metal with the highest melting point of any element — tungsten, at 3,422 degrees Celsius — which can be run white-hot without boiling itself away. T2: the name is an insult. Saxon tin miners hated the ore because it devoured the tin they were trying to smelt, and Agricola in 1546 called it lupi spuma, 'wolf's froth', for eating the tin like a wolf. That is why the metal is wolfram across much of Europe and why its symbol is W. Scheele identified the acid in 1781; the brothers Juan Jose and Fausto Elhuyar reduced it with charcoal and isolated the metal in Spain in 1783. T3: the obstacle was never the melting point — it was BRITTLENESS. Alexander Just and Franz Hanaman's Hungarian patent of 1904 made tungsten filaments by pressing and firing a paste of tungsten powder; they lit beautifully and they snapped. William Coolidge at General Electric spent years on the problem and by 1910 had a working process for tungsten ductile enough to be drawn into wire six micrometres across, kilometres at a time. T4: in 1913 Irving Langmuir at GE fixed the last of it by changing what surrounded the filament rather than the filament — he stopped pumping bulbs to vacuum and filled them with argon or nitrogen, which slows the tungsten's evaporation, then coiled the wire so the gas around it carries away less heat.
source: Wikipedia 'Tungsten' (melting point 3,422 C, the highest of any element; Scheele's tungstic acid 1781; the Elhuyar brothers' 1783 isolation by charcoal reduction at the Royal Basque Society; Agricola's 1546 'lupi spuma' and the wolfram/W etymology); Wikipedia 'Alexander Just' and rbs0.com 'History of Incandescent Electric Lamps in the USA' (the Just-Hanaman Hungarian patent effective 7 October 1904, brittle pressed-powder filaments); American Scientist, "Tungsten's Brilliant, Hidden History" and 100 Years of Doped Tungsten Wire (Coolidge's ductile-tungsten process by 1910, drawn wire ~6 micrometres, GE 'Mazda'); GE/Langmuir accounts of the 1913 gas-filled and coiled filament lamps.
framing_note: Voice: MECHANISM mode — a short, satisfying engineering ladder where each rung is a DIFFERENT obstacle, not a repeat. T1 keys the property (a metal you can run white-hot), never 'who invented the lightbulb', which is a different and much-contested question this ladder must stay out of. Accuracy rails: do not credit Edison with the tungsten filament — he used carbon and later bamboo; the tungsten line runs Just and Hanaman (1904, brittle) to Coolidge (1910, ductile) to Langmuir (1913, gas fill and coil). Do not say tungsten 'does not melt'; say it melts higher than any other element and give the number once. Dinner-test payoff: T2 — the metal is named after miners cursing it for eating their tin. Distractor mine: the real filament materials that were actually tried and lost (carbon, carbonised bamboo, platinum, osmium, tantalum, molybdenum) — each a genuine commercial filament at some point. Keep the ladder short; do not pad it with modern applications.
history_overlap: HISTORY bank: wolfram supply and Portuguese neutrality in the Second World War is a war-economy episode that bank owns — do not go near it. Internal SCIENCE overlap: an electricity/invention sub-strand may own Edison, Swan and the incandescent-lamp priority fight; this ladder must stay on the ELEMENT and its two failure modes, and cede the who-invented-the-bulb question entirely.
